items.title: 20 Truths about Life from 20 Years of The Marginalian: A Ceramics and Lichen Raffle
items.description: It is an odd thing, looking back on your life, trying to recognize in the mirror of memory the people you used to be, finding them strangers: the person who kissed your first kiss, the person who drank your last drink, the person who had your best idea, the person who made your worst mistake, the person who over and over mistook fear for love, the person who thought orange was a good idea. items.title: How to Hold Your Heart with Golden Hands
items.description: One bleak English winter a long time ago, wandering through London in the wake of a relationship that had just unraveled, I walked into an antiquarian bookstore and chanced upon a rare century-old edition of the Brothers Grimm fairy tales — which I had grown up with — illustrated by Arthur Rackham. items.title: Ursula K. Le Guin on the Meaning of Life
items.description: We are the survivors of immense and minute events — violent cosmic collisions and subtle genetic mutations, the deaths of innumerable suns and the births of innumerable cells, the splitting of continents and the splitting of atoms. Out of it all, we emerged as creatures muzzled by a consciousness that demands we give meaning to our survival. It will not come like alms dropped from the unfeeling hand of the universe. items.title: Nathaniel Hawthorne on How to Look and Really See
items.description: "The mystery is revealed, and after a breath or two, becomes just as great a mystery as before."

items.title: How to Unself in Order to Be Who You Really Are
items.description: "The self, the place where we live, is a place of illusion. Goodness is connected with the attempt to see the unself... to pierce the veil of selfish consciousness and join the world as it really is."

items.title: Corrective for a Broken Heart
items.description: “Life will break you,” Louise Erdrich wrote in her passionate insistence that “you are here to risk your heart.” It can happen with a shattering, or with a thousand small fissures, but the great paradox — the great salvation — is that every time it happens, you live to see you are unbreakable. And so, a poem. CORRECTIVE FOR A BROKEN HEART by Maria Popova Why all the threadbare drama, the stale catastrophism of calling it broken? items.title: How to Be Un-Dead: Notes on Waking Up from the Trance of Near-Living
items.description: "Life is a process of becoming, a combination of states we have to go through. Where people fail is that they wish to elect a state and remain in it. This is a kind of death."

items.title: How to Grow Old without Letting Life Become a Parody of Itself
items.description: "In old age we should wish still to have passions strong enough to prevent us turning in on ourselves."

items.title: The Wildest Bet Is the Winning Bet
items.description: We place life’s bets by countless calculations of probability, conscious and unconscious, only to discover over and over how short they fall of the wildest reaches of the possible, which always includes but exceeds the probable. It helps to remember that we ourselves are children of improbability, that everything we treasure exists not because it had to, not because it was likely or necessary, but because the universe took a gamble against the staggering odds otherwise. items.title: How to Be Transformed When Things Fall Apart
items.description: "Only to the extent that we expose ourselves over and over to annihilation can that which is indestructible be found in us."

items.title: How to Stop Waiting and Start Living: A Jolt from Henry James
items.description: "It wouldn't have been failure to be bankrupt, dishonoured, pilloried, hanged; it was failure not to be anything."

items.title: Introducing the Museum of Delight
items.description: After twenty years of making immaterial things with my mind — ideas sculpted of words, questions woven of sentences, translucent vessels for thought and feeling in the shape of poems — I found myself overcome by the urge to make things with my hands out of matter: clay, thread, stone, resin, wood, lichen. items.title: Love After Life: Nobel-Winning Physicist Richard Feynman’s Extraordinary Letter to His Departed Wife
items.description: Where the hard edge of physics meets the vulnerable metaphysics of the human heart.

items.title: When Relationships Change: Anne Morrow Lindbergh on Embracing the Intermittency and Mutability of Love
items.description: "All living relationships are in process of change, of expansion, and must perpetually be building themselves new forms."

items.title: The Constitution of the Inner Country: Leonard Cohen on Language and the Poetry of Presence
items.description: "The poem is nothing but information. It is the Constitution of the inner country."
